newsitem.title: USA: UPS, union resume talks as shipments slow.
newsitem.headline: UPS, union resume talks as shipments slow.

text.p: United Parcel Service and the Teamsters union resumed talking on Friday in an effort to avoid a strike at the huge package carrier.
"At this point we are diligently working," UPS spokeswoman Gina Ellrich told reporters before the talks began. "The mood is absolutely serious -- it's very businesslike."

Teamsters President Ron Carey, entering the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service offices in Washington, said he was optimistic but warned: "If we fail to find some solution to these issues then we will be on strike."

A four-year contract between UPS and the International Brotherhood of Teamsters expired at midnight (0400 GMT) on Thursday, but the union postponed any action to allow for further talks. The two sides met through the night before taking a break early this morning.
The negotiations cover a range of issues, the union said, including the creation of more full-time jobs, an end to subcontracting, safety, health and pension issues.

A strike against the company could throw the country's package delivery service into chaos, stranding more than 12 million parcels destined for about 1.5 million U.S. customers a day. It would also put about 200,000 Teamsters out of work.
UPS said Friday the strike threat had already caused it to lose out on a substantial quantity of its delivery business.
"We have literally lost hundreds of thousands of packages in terms of those being diverted to competitors, many of which are non-union shops," spokeswoman Jennifer Jiles said.
Otherwise, Jiles said that the company was operating normally, and money-back guarantees still applied to time-sensitive deliveries such as next-day and second-day air.
On Tuesday, the company notified customers that it could not guarantee delivery once the contract expired.

The company is the largest package carrier in the country with 1996 revenues of $22.4 billion. It handles 3.15 billion parcels and documents shipped annually to more than 200 countries from 1,700 hubs and centers.

"UPS ships more than all the other carriers combined. There simply are not enough other carriers to pick up the slack," Kathy Luhn, a spokeswoman with the National Industrial Transportation League, a Virginia-based trade association said on Thursday.
Drug companies said a UPS strike could pose a threat to the delivery of drugs and medical supplies to hospitals and eventually could affect critically ill patients.

"It's a major concern for us because it affects how we are going to get our medications to the people who need them, particularly critically ill patients," said Amy Magan, a spokesman for pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly and Co..
The Teamsters' Carey said both sides would begin their latest meeting by reviewing their respective positions.
"It's not an easy process and there are no simple solutions," he said.
Ellrich said there had been no further developments in the talks and reiterated that UPS had made its "last, best and final" offer.
